title: GOD CURSED THIS SIN BY NAME—BUT WHY? THE DISTURBING SECRET BEHIND DEUTERONOMY 27:23
paragraphs: GOD CURSED THIS SIN BY NAME—BUT WHY? THE DISTURBING SECRET BEHIND DEUTERONOMY 27:23

One forbidden relationship. One terrifying declaration from Mount Ebal. And one uncomfortable truth about family, hidden sin, and the holiness of God that reaches far beyond the ancient world. But the most astonishing part of this story is not the curse. It is what Jesus Christ came to do for people living under the weight of sin.
There are Bible verses that comfort you.
There are Bible verses that strengthen you.
And then there are Bible verses that make you stop reading, stare at the page, and whisper…
“Lord, why is THAT in the Bible?”
Deuteronomy 27:23 is one of them.

Imagine standing among thousands of Israelites in the land God promised their ancestors. Families are gathered. Children are listening. The Levites are speaking with authority. The entire nation is being reminded that their covenant with God is not a religious performance.
It is a matter of life and death.
Then, suddenly, a particular curse is announced.
“Cursed be he that lieth with his mother in law. And all the people shall say, Amen.” — Deuteronomy 27:23, KJV
Read that again.
Not a general warning against sexual immorality.
Not a vague command about inappropriate relationships.
God specifically identifies sexual intercourse with a mother-in-law.
And the entire congregation must answer:
“Amen.”
Why?
Why would the Lord of heaven and earth single out something so disturbing?
Was this happening in ancient Israel? Was there a deeper cultural reason? Was God protecting marriage, family boundaries, or something much greater?
And what does an ancient curse about a mother-in-law have to do with the person reading this article today?
Perhaps more than we would like to admit.
Because before this passage confronts the scandal inside a family, it exposes something far more universal.
The human heart has an astonishing ability to justify what God has forbidden.
And sometimes the most dangerous sins are not committed by strangers.
They happen behind doors that everyone assumes are safe.
The Hebrew text makes the prohibition unmistakable.
אָרוּר שֹׁכֵב עִם־חֹתַנְתּו וְאָמַר כָּל־הָעָם אָמֵן
ʾĀrūr šōkhēḇ ʿim-ḥōṯantō; wəʾāmar kol-hāʿām ʾāmēn.
A close English rendering is:
“Cursed is the one who lies with his mother-in-law. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
The word אָרוּר (ʾārūr) means “cursed,” expressing a solemn declaration of judgment.
The expression שֹׁכֵב עִם (šōkhēḇ ʿim) literally means “lying with,” a biblical expression that in this context refers to sexual intercourse.
And חֹתַנְתּו (ḥōṯantō) identifies his mother-in-law.
There is no mysterious alternate meaning that transforms this into an innocent family disagreement.
There is no hidden Hebrew metaphor about disrespecting your wife's mother.
The verse is addressing a prohibited sexual relationship.
But understanding the Hebrew is only the beginning.
To understand why this curse appears, we must enter the world of the covenant.
In Deuteronomy 27, Moses instructs Israel about a solemn ceremony to take place after entering the promised land.
The people are to stand in relation to Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, with blessings and curses publicly declared.
This is not merely a collection of strange ancient laws.
It is a national confrontation with covenant responsibility.
The people who have experienced God's deliverance must now understand what faithfulness to Him requires.
And notice something fascinating about the curses in Deuteronomy 27.

They address idolatry, dishonoring parents, stealing a neighbor's land, misleading the blind, perverting justice, prohibited sexual relationships, secret violence, bribery, and failure to uphold God's law.
These are not random offenses.
They expose the ways people betray God and harm one another, often while maintaining an appearance of respectability.
Consider Deuteronomy 27:15, which condemns the making of an idol and setting it up “in a secret place.”
Or verse 24, which condemns someone who strikes a neighbor secretly.
The repeated concern with concealed wrongdoing helps us recognize a broader pattern.
God's covenant standards do not stop at the front door.
They enter the private life.
They confront the things a community might never discover.
They reach the places where human witnesses are absent.
And that should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because we know what it feels like to have a public version of ourselves and a private version.
We know how easily a person can appear faithful on Sunday while fighting temptations no one else can see.
We know how families sometimes protect appearances instead of confronting wrongdoing.
And we know that the sentence “Nobody will ever find out” has preceded countless tragedies.
But Scripture refuses to confuse secrecy with innocence.
What is hidden from people is never hidden from God.
Now look at the closely related law in Leviticus.
Leviticus 18:17 forbids sexual relations involving a woman and her daughter, identifying the relationship as a violation of family boundaries.
Leviticus 20:14 addresses a man who takes a woman and her mother, prescribing a severe punishment under Israel's ancient covenant law.
These passages belong to a wider body of legislation defining forbidden sexual relationships and protecting the boundaries of kinship and marriage.
The biblical text does not tell us that Deuteronomy 27:23 was introduced because of one documented incident involving a particular Israelite family.
We should not invent a scandal the Bible never records.
What we can say is that the law explicitly prohibits this relationship, and its placement among the covenant curses communicates its seriousness.
In biblical ethics, marriage does not erase all family boundaries.
A mother-in-law is not simply another unrelated adult available for sexual pursuit.
She belongs to a family relationship that must be honored rather than sexualized.
And violating that boundary can produce betrayal across generations.
Imagine the devastation.
A daughter discovers that the husband she trusted has become sexually involved with her own mother.
A marriage is shattered.
A mother-daughter relationship is deeply wounded.
Trust collapses inside the family.
People who should have protected one another become sources of profound pain.
And the consequences may reach children, relatives, and an entire household.
That is not merely a private romantic choice.
It is a betrayal of relationships that carry moral responsibilities.
This helps explain why the biblical prohibition matters.
God is not treating human sexuality as something dirty.
Scripture presents marital intimacy as good and honorable within its proper covenant setting.
Genesis 2:24 describes a man leaving his father and mother and being joined to his wife, with the two becoming one flesh.
Hebrews 13:4 calls marriage honorable and warns against sexual immorality and adultery.
The problem in Deuteronomy 27:23 is not that sexual intimacy exists.
The problem is that intimacy has crossed a boundary God forbids.
A sacred gift has been misused.
And when something designed for covenant faithfulness becomes an instrument of betrayal, the damage can be devastating.
But there is another detail in this verse that deserves our attention.
The people must respond:
אָמֵן — ʾāmēn.
This Hebrew word communicates affirmation, certainty, and agreement.
In this setting, the people are publicly acknowledging the righteousness and authority of the covenant declaration.
They are not being asked to enjoy the punishment of another human being.
They are being called to affirm that God's standards matter.
Even when those standards expose sins that people might prefer to ignore.
And here is where the passage becomes painfully personal.
It is easy to say “Amen” when the sin being condemned belongs to someone else.
It is easy to agree with God's holiness when the person under examination is a stranger.
It is easy to become outraged by a scandal that does not threaten our own reputation.
But what happens when Scripture turns toward us?
What happens when Jesus confronts our own lust, dishonesty, pride, bitterness, selfishness, or secret compromise?
Do we still say “Amen”?
Or do we begin searching for excuses?
Jesus intensifies this examination in Matthew 5:27–28.
He reminds His listeners of the commandment against adultery and then teaches that looking at someone with lustful intent already exposes adultery in the heart.
That does not mean every temptation is identical to committing a physical act, nor does it erase the different harms and consequences of different sins.
It means God's concern reaches beyond outward behavior into the desires we deliberately entertain.
A person may never violate the specific prohibition in Deuteronomy 27:23 and still desperately need God's mercy.
The ancient verse is not permission to feel morally superior.
It is an invitation to examine our own hearts before the Lord.
And this is where the story takes an unexpected turn.
Because the Bible that announces curses against sin is also the Bible that reveals a Savior who bears the curse for sinners.
Listen carefully.
Deuteronomy does not end with the conclusion that sinful people can save themselves by trying harder.
The larger biblical story moves toward Jesus Christ.
Paul writes in Galatians 3:10 about the curse associated with failure to continue in everything written in the Law.
Then comes one of the most breathtaking declarations in the New Testament.
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.” — Galatians 3:13, KJV
The Greek text begins:
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law.”
The verb ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen) expresses the act of redeeming or buying out of bondage.
And κατάρα (katara) means “curse.”
Paul is not teaching that Jesus became morally sinful.
He is declaring that Christ bore the curse on behalf of His people through His crucifixion.
The innocent Savior took upon Himself the judgment that sinners could never overcome through their own righteousness.
Do you see the wonder?
In Deuteronomy 27, the people hear the solemn declaration:
“Cursed.”
In Galatians 3, believers hear the astonishing announcement:
“Christ redeemed us.”
The Gospel does not say that God's holiness was exaggerated.
It does not say sin was harmless after all.
It does not say betrayal no longer matters.
It says something infinitely more costly.
The Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
The cross is not God pretending evil never happened.
It is the revelation of His justice and mercy in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because there are people reading this who carry memories they have never spoken aloud.
Perhaps you crossed a boundary you knew was wrong.
Perhaps you betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps you were involved in a relationship that wounded your family.
Perhaps you have lived for years with guilt, shame, or the fear of being exposed.
Or perhaps you are the one who was betrayed.
You trusted someone.
You believed your family was safe.
You thought the people closest to you would protect your heart.
And instead, they became part of the reason it broke.
If that is your story, hear this carefully.
The guilt belongs to the person who committed the wrong.
If you were coerced, exploited, or abused, you are not responsible for another person's sin against you.
The commandment condemns wrongdoing; it does not condemn its victims.
And forgiveness must never be twisted into a demand that victims remain in danger, abandon necessary boundaries, or silence the truth.
Jesus does not require us to call evil good.
He calls sinners to repentance, offers grace to the broken, and teaches His people to walk in truth.
For the person who has committed serious sin, repentance is not merely feeling bad because consequences have arrived.
It is turning away from sin and turning toward God.
It means ending the forbidden relationship.
It means refusing to continue the deception.
It means taking responsibility without blaming the person who was harmed.
It means pursuing appropriate accountability and accepting that reconciliation may require time, boundaries, and consequences.
And where abuse or criminal wrongdoing has occurred, repentance does not replace the need for protection or lawful accountability.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying lives.
Grace is the mercy of God that calls us out of darkness and into the light.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers wanted to use her situation as a trap.
Jesus confronted their self-righteousness without declaring sin acceptable.
And after the accusers departed, He told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Notice both parts.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy and holiness.
Forgiveness and transformation.
Grace that receives the sinner without celebrating the sin.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus does not offer us a new name for our rebellion so that we can remain unchanged.
He offers forgiveness and a new life.
And that is why the words of 1 John 1:9 are so precious.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
The promise is not that confession will erase every earthly consequence.
It is that God's forgiveness and cleansing are available through Jesus Christ.
No human scandal is too complicated for God to understand.
No hidden sin is beyond His knowledge.
And no repentant sinner must conclude that Christ's mercy is insufficient.
That does not make sin small.
It makes the Savior glorious.
Perhaps the most haunting question in Deuteronomy 27:23 is not why God named this particular sin.
Perhaps it is why we are so quick to recognize the ugliness of someone else's wrongdoing while minimizing our own.
We see betrayal and cry for justice.
We see hypocrisy and demand exposure.
We see scandal and wonder how anyone could do such a thing.
But when God examines our own hearts, do we welcome His truth?
Or do we hide?
Remember Adam and Eve in Genesis 3.
After disobeying God, they hid.
Sin had introduced shame, fear, and alienation.
And the Lord called to Adam:
“Where art thou?”
God was not lacking information.
The question confronted Adam with his condition.
And throughout Scripture, that same searching reality remains.
Where are you?
Not geographically.
Spiritually.
Where are you standing before God?
Behind excuses?
Behind religious appearances?
Behind the approval of people who do not know what happens in private?
Behind the sentence, “At least I am not as bad as that person”?
Or are you finally willing to come into the light?
The Gospel invitation is not to pretend you have never fallen.
It is to come to the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
Jesus Christ was crucified for our sins, buried, and raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures, as Paul proclaims in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Our hope is not in our ability to rewrite our own past.
Our hope is in the crucified and risen Savior.
The same Jesus who calls us to repent is the Jesus who welcomes the weary.
The same Lord who exposes darkness offers the light of life.
And the same Gospel that declares forgiveness also creates a people who learn to honor marriage, protect the vulnerable, tell the truth, and live in holiness.
That is why this difficult passage still deserves to be read.
Not because shocking sexual scandals are entertaining.
Not because the church needs another reason to humiliate broken people.
But because God's Word tells the truth about sin, even when that truth is uncomfortable.
And because the greater story of Scripture leads us to the One who can redeem what sin has devastated.
Maybe someone you love needs to hear this.
Not to be publicly accused.
Not to be embarrassed.
But to be reminded that hidden compromise is dangerous and that genuine repentance is possible.

You do not need to disclose private details, name people who harmed you, or make a public confession to receive God's forgiveness. A simple prayer, a Scripture, or a word of encouragement may be exactly what another reader needs.
Because people do not merely need religious inspiration.
We need the truth that leads us to Jesus.
If this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, confront sin, rediscover grace, or grow closer to Christ, I also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is working to continue and expand its ministry of biblical teaching, Gospel-centered encouragement, and discipleship resources.
These resources are intended to help believers study the Word, strengthen their faith, grow in spiritual maturity, and remain rooted in the Gospel.
And keeping this work going requires time, resources, and faithful support.
Not because God's love can be purchased.
Not because giving money proves someone is a better Christian.
But because believers are free to support Gospel ministry generously, willingly, and with joy.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You can glorify God through faithfulness, generosity, service, love, and obedience in countless ways.
No one needs to pay to belong to Christ.
No one needs to purchase access to His mercy.
But when believers freely come together to support sound biblical teaching, they can help bring that message to more people.
Perhaps someone reading the next article will finally open a Bible.
Perhaps someone who has been hiding in shame will find the courage to seek help and repent.
Perhaps a wounded believer will discover that Jesus has not abandoned them.
Perhaps a family will begin rebuilding on truth rather than secrecy.
We cannot manufacture those outcomes.
But we can faithfully proclaim the Gospel and entrust the results to God.
And now, before you leave, return with me one last time to that ancient gathering in Deuteronomy.
The people stand beneath the solemn weight of God's covenant.
A curse is declared against a sin that violates the sacred boundaries of family.
The congregation answers:
“Amen.”
Generations pass.
Israel's story unfolds through faithfulness and rebellion, judgment and mercy, exile and restoration.
Then, outside Jerusalem, the sinless Son of God hangs upon a Roman cross.
The crowd sees suffering.
His enemies see defeat.
But the apostles will proclaim something far greater.
Christ has redeemed His people from the curse of the law.
He has given Himself for sinners.
And through His death and resurrection, the way of forgiveness and reconciliation with God has been opened.
That is the difference between a message that merely exposes scandal and the Gospel that announces grace.
The law reveals the seriousness of sin.
The cross reveals the astonishing cost of redemption.
And the resurrection declares that death does not have the final word.
So do not leave this passage merely thinking about somebody else's forbidden relationship.
Ask what God is teaching you about holiness.
Ask where your own heart needs repentance.
Ask whether you have mistaken secrecy for safety.
Ask whether you have allowed shame to convince you that Jesus could never receive you.
And remember the promise of Romans 8:1:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That is not a declaration that sin does not matter.
It is the glorious announcement that those who belong to Christ are no longer under condemnation.
The curse is real.
The cross is real.
The resurrection is real.
And the grace of God in Jesus Christ is more powerful than the shame of a past that has been brought into His light.
The sin you were afraid to bring into the light may be the very place where you finally discover how desperately you need the Savior who never stopped calling you out of the darkness.
